canonical_topic: Taxonomy of Financial Instruments: Real Assets, Financial Assets, Derivatives
definition: Trading centers on financial instruments (securities), which fall into three types: real assets (physical commodities like crude oil, electricity, gold, plus legislatively created rights like carbon emissions rights), financial assets (contracts conferring an ownership interest in a company — stocks — a lien on a company — bonds — or currencies), and derivatives (contracts whose value is derived from other financial instruments). To count as a financial instrument, an asset must be tradable, meaning it can be legally assigned to someone else for a cash payment.
core_idea: Nearly all energy market transactions take the form of derivatives rather than direct trades of the physical commodity or of financial assets.
key_points: Real assets = physical commodities + legislatively created rights (e.g., carbon emissions rights).
Financial assets = ownership interest (stocks), a lien on a company (bonds), or currencies.
Derivatives = contracts that derive their value from other financial instruments; the vast majority of energy transactions fall in this category.
Tradability requirement: an asset must be legally assignable to another party for a cash payment to qualify as a financial instrument.
trading_implications: Because most energy exposure is taken via derivatives rather than physical assets, understanding the underlying instrument a derivative references is central to trading it.
